lessons.title: Policies, standards, procedures: the documentation pyramid
objectives: Tell apart policy, internal standard, baseline, guideline and procedure.
Know what is mandatory and what is recommended.
Know the types of policies and how exceptions are managed.

references.title: NIST SP 800-12 Rev. 1, An Introduction to Information Security (chapter on policies)

blocks.text: From "why" to "how"

An organization's security rests on a set of nested documents. At the top, few documents, very stable and approved by management; at the bottom, many detailed documents that change often along with the technology.

blocks.title: The documentation pyramid
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram from the most general to the most detailed: policy, internal standard, baseline, procedure. Guidelines, which are optional, sit apart.
blocks.text: Guidelines advise without obliging: they stay beside the pyramid.

rows: "Remote access is protected by strong authentication."
"MFA is mandatory, using an authenticator app or a FIDO2 key."
Minimum configuration level for a type of system
Hardened Windows Server configuration: services disabled, logging enabled
Detailed steps to carry out a task, the "how"
Step-by-step procedure for creating a VPN account

blocks.text: The policy is short, written in general terms and signed by management: it gives authority to the documents derived from it. A standard that sets "14 characters minimum" changes more often than a policy, so technical details are kept out of the policy.
Policy = WHY · Standard = WHAT (with figures) · Procedure = HOW. Only the guideline says "I advise you".
Types of policies

items: General (or program) policy: defines the security program, the roles and the CISO's authority.
Issue-specific policy: deals with one topic, for example remote work, acceptable use, removable media.
System-specific policy: rules for a given system, for example who may change the SIEM configuration.

blocks.text: This three-type classification is presented in particular by NIST SP 800-12.
Exceptions

A requirement cannot always be met (legacy application, business constraint). Rather than leaving the gap hidden, an exception is requested: it is justified, limited in time, backed by compensating controls and approved by the risk owner. It is recorded in a register and reviewed when it expires.

blocks.title: The forgotten exception
blocks.text: An exception without an end date becomes a permanent hole. The exceptions register must be reviewed, otherwise nobody remembers the server that was "temporarily" exempted three years ago.

blocks.title: SOC case: when the procedure is missing
blocks.text: One night, an analyst discovers a suspicious login on an executive's account. The policy says that "incidents are handled according to their severity", the standard sets the severity levels, but no procedure explains how to reset the account of an executive who is traveling. The analyst loses an hour looking for whom to call. Lesson learned: write a procedure (the "how") with the contacts and the steps, and test it.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I keep the policy short and stable, and I keep the standards and procedures alive.
SOC manager: I want precise procedures (playbooks) that can be used at 3 a.m.
Auditor: I check that every document is approved, dated, distributed and applied.
Risk manager: I follow the exceptions register and its deadlines.

blocks.text: To classify a document in the exam, look for figures: "at least 16 characters" is a standard, "protect access" is a policy, "click Isolate then call the on-call engineer" is a procedure.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: The guideline is the only non-mandatory document.
The policy says "why" and "what" at a high level; the procedure says "how".
The baseline is a mandatory minimum, not a recommendation.
A policy is approved by management, not by the technical team.
Policy → standards → baselines → procedures; guidelines advise.
Three types of policies: general, issue-specific, system-specific.
An exception is justified, temporary, compensated, approved and tracked.

lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a four-story colored pyramid with a small flag on top.

lessons.title: The ISO/IEC 27000 family and the ISMS
objectives: Place the main standards of the ISO/IEC 27000 family.
Describe the structure of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and its Annex A.
Explain the statement of applicability and the certification cycle.

references.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, information security management system requirements

blocks.text: A family of standards

rows: Requirements for an ISMS: an ISMS is certified against it
Controls for the cloud; protection of personal data in the public cloud
Identification, collection and preservation of digital evidence
Privacy information management (personal data), also certifiable

blocks.text: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the ISMS

blocks.title: ISMS, Information Security Management System (SMSI)
blocks.text: Organized set of policies, processes, roles and resources for managing information security systematically and improving it continuously.

rows: Internal and external issues, interested parties, ISMS scope
Management commitment, policy, roles and responsibilities
Risk assessment and treatment, security objectives
Resources, competence, awareness, communication, documented information
Implementation of the plans and of risk treatment
Monitoring, measurement, internal audit, management review

blocks.text: These clauses follow the logic of continual improvement often summed up by the PDCA cycle (Plan, Do, Check, Act): plan (6), do (8), check (9), act (10). Since the 2013 version, the standard no longer imposes PDCA as a model, but the logic remains.

blocks.title: The PDCA logic in ISO/IEC 27001
blocks.alt: Four-step cycle: Plan (clause 6, planning), Do (clause 8, operation), Check (clause 9, performance evaluation), Act (clause 10, improvement), then start again.

blocks.text: Annex A and the statement of applicability

Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 lists 93 controls in four themes: organizational (37), people (8), physical (14) and technological (34). ISO/IEC 27002:2022 details each of them. The 2013 version had 114 controls in 14 domains; the transition period to the 2022 version ended on 31 October 2025.

blocks.title: The 93 Annex A controls (2022)
blocks.alt: Bar chart: 37 organizational controls, 8 people controls, 14 physical, 34 technological, 93 in total.
blocks.text: 37 + 8 + 14 + 34 = 93. Former 2013 version: 114 controls in 14 domains.
"27000 Defines, 27001 Requires, 27002 Guides, 27005 Risk": the vocabulary, the certifiable requirements, the controls guide, risk management.

blocks.title: SoA, Statement of Applicability (déclaration d'applicabilité)
blocks.text: Mandatory document that lists all Annex A controls, states whether each one is applied or excluded, and justifies that choice in the light of risk treatment.

blocks.title: Certification cycle
items: Initial audit in two stages: documentation review (stage 1), then verification of implementation (stage 2).
Certificate valid for three years.
Surveillance audits (usually yearly) during those three years.
Recertification audit before expiry.

blocks.title: Key point
blocks.text: You get certified to ISO/IEC 27001, never to ISO/IEC 27002: 27002 is a guide that helps implement the controls, it contains no requirements to audit.

blocks.title: SOC case: the SOC within the ISMS
blocks.text: During her employer's 27001 audit, the SOC manager has to show that the logging and monitoring controls of Annex A are applied. She presents the logging policy, the list of sources connected to the SIEM, handled incident tickets and the monthly indicator report. The auditor also asks for proof that lessons from incidents feed improvement (clause 10).

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: certification is not the goal; the ISMS is there to steer risks over time.
SOC manager: my tickets and indicators are valuable audit evidence.
Auditor: without a management review or an internal audit, the ISMS is not compliant.
Risk manager: the SoA must follow from risk treatment, not the other way round.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: You get certified to ISO/IEC 27001, not to 27002 (which is a guide).
Annex A 2022: 93 controls, 4 themes. Former 2013 version: 114 controls, 14 domains.
The SoA also justifies exclusions.
Management has explicit obligations (clause 5 Leadership, management review in clause 9).
27000 vocabulary, 27001 requirements (certifiable), 27002 controls, 27005 risks.
27001:2022: clauses 4 to 10, Annex A with 93 controls in 4 themes.
Mandatory SoA; 3-year certificate with surveillance audits.

lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a certificate with a seal and a ribbon, next to a three-year calendar.

lessons.title: Other frameworks: NIST, COBIT, PCI DSS, SOC 2, ANSSI
objectives: List the six functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0.
Place NIST SP 800-53, COBIT, ITIL, PCI DSS and SOC 2.
Choose a framework according to the need.

references.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

blocks.text: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0

Published in 2024, CSF 2.0 organizes cybersecurity into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. It is not certifiable: it is a framework to describe your current level, set a target level and prioritize.

rows: Who decides, and following which strategy?
What must be protected, and against what?
Inventory of the assets connected to the SIEM
How do we prevent the incident?
How do we get back to normal?

blocks.text: Other useful frameworks

rows: Detailed catalog of security and privacy controls
Choose and describe controls (US public sector and beyond)
Align IT with the business objectives
Mandatory for anyone who stores, processes or transmits card data
Audit report on a service provider's controls
Reassure the customers of a service provider, especially in the cloud
Guides and methods of the French agency
IT hygiene guide (42 measures), EBIOS Risk Manager method

blocks.text: A SOC 2 Type I report describes the design of the controls at a given date; a Type II report also assesses how they actually operated over a period (often 6 to 12 months). Be careful not to confuse SOC 2 (audit report) with a SOC (security operations center).
SOC 2 Type I = a photo (the controls are well designed on a given date). SOC 2 Type II = a film (they worked for 6 to 12 months).

blocks.title: Common confusion
blocks.text: SOC 2 is an audit report on a service provider; a SOC is a security operations center. A question that talks about a "report", an "auditor" or a "period" is about SOC 2.
Choosing and combining

Frameworks complement each other: ISO/IEC 27001 for the management system, ISO/IEC 27002 or NIST SP 800-53 for the controls, NIST CSF to communicate a maturity level, PCI DSS if you handle cards, EBIOS Risk Manager for risk analysis. Mapping tables exist between most of them.

blocks.title: Combining frameworks
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: ISO/IEC 27001 for the management system, ISO/IEC 27002 or NIST SP 800-53 to choose the controls, NIST CSF to communicate maturity, PCI DSS if you handle bank cards.

blocks.title: SOC case: a customer demands evidence
blocks.text: An MSSP (outsourced SOC) answers a bank's call for tenders. The bank asks for ISO/IEC 27001 certification and a SOC 2 Type II report covering the last twelve months, and points out that the scope handles card data subject to PCI DSS. The provider's SOC manager must supply evidence that the controls operate: logs, tickets, access reviews.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I choose one main framework and map the others to it to avoid duplication.
SOC manager: the NIST CSF helps me show management our Detect and Respond coverage.
Auditor: a SOC 2 Type II report is worth more than a Type I to judge effectiveness.
Risk manager: EBIOS Risk Manager structures risk scenarios with the business units.

blocks.text: Remember one question to ask about every framework: "is it certifiable?". ISO/IEC 27001 yes, the NIST CSF no, PCI DSS leads to a compliance assessment, SOC 2 to an audit report.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, including Govern added in 2.0.
The NIST CSF is not certifiable; ISO/IEC 27001 is.
PCI DSS is an industry standard (payment cards), not a law.
SOC 2 Type I = design at a date; Type II = effectiveness over a period.
ITIL manages IT services; COBIT governs IT.
NIST CSF 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
SP 800-53: controls catalog; COBIT: IT governance; ITIL: services.
PCI DSS for cards; SOC 2 to reassure a provider's customers.
ANSSI: hygiene guide (42 measures), EBIOS Risk Manager.

lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of an open toolbox containing colored cards: each framework is a tool.

questions.prompt: Which document expresses senior management's security intentions and principles in general terms?
questions.explanation: The policy, approved by senior management, sets the principles and gives authority to the other documents.

whyNot.0: The procedure describes the steps of a task, the "how".
whyNot.1: The baseline sets a minimum configuration for a type of system.
whyNot.2: The guideline is a non-mandatory recommendation.

questions.prompt: Which of these documents is NOT mandatory?
questions.explanation: The guideline gives advice; it is recommended but not mandatory.

whyNot.0: The policy applies to everyone.
whyNot.2: The procedure describes the mandatory way to carry out a task.
whyNot.3: The internal standard sets mandatory, measurable requirements.

questions.prompt: "Passwords for privileged accounts have at least 16 characters." This text is typically:
questions.explanation: It is a precise, measurable requirement: it belongs to an internal standard, which derives from the policy.

whyNot.0: A policy stays general and avoids technical details that change often.
whyNot.1: The text is mandatory, not a recommendation.
whyNot.2: A procedure would describe the steps to, for example, change a password.

questions.prompt: A minimum hardened configuration imposed on all production Linux servers is called:
questions.explanation: A baseline sets the minimum mandatory security level for a type of system.

whyNot.0: An issue-specific policy addresses a topic in general terms, not a detailed configuration.
whyNot.1: A guideline would not be imposed.
whyNot.3: An exception is an authorized deviation from a requirement, the opposite of an imposed minimum.

questions.prompt: Which document describes step by step how to isolate a compromised workstation from the EDR console?
questions.explanation: The procedure describes the "how": the precise steps of a task. In the SOC, it is often called a playbook.

whyNot.0: A guideline advises; it does not describe a mandatory course of action.
whyNot.1: The internal standard sets a requirement, not the operating method.
whyNot.3: The policy gives the principles, not the steps.

questions.prompt: A policy governing the use of USB drives across the whole company is a policy that is:
questions.explanation: It addresses a specific topic for the whole organization: it is an issue-specific policy.

whyNot.0: The general policy defines the security program as a whole.
whyNot.1: A system-specific policy sets the rules of a given system.
whyNot.3: Business continuity is a different topic.

questions.prompt: What conditions must a valid exception to a security standard meet? (2 answers)
choices: Be limited in time and reviewed when it expires
Be approved by the risk owner, with compensating measures
Remain confidential and kept out of any register
Be granted verbally by the technical team
questions.explanation: An exception is justified, temporary, compensated, approved by an authorized person and tracked in a register.

whyNot.2: A hidden exception prevents the risk from being tracked; it must be recorded.
whyNot.3: A verbal exception from the technical team has neither a record nor sufficient authority.

questions.prompt: Why do we avoid writing detailed technical settings in the security policy?
choices: Because a policy is not mandatory and can be ignored
Because the policy must remain stable while settings change often
Because senior management must not know these settings
Because the law forbids putting technical details in it
questions.explanation: A policy approved by senior management must last. Technical details change often; they are placed in standards and procedures to avoid having the policy reapproved at each change.

whyNot.0: The policy is mandatory.
whyNot.2: It is not about hiding anything from senior management.
whyNot.3: No law imposes this split: it is a good practice.

questions.prompt: Who approves the information security policy?
questions.explanation: The policy commits the organization: it is approved by senior management, which gives it its authority.

whyNot.0: An external vendor has no authority over the policy.
whyNot.2: Employees read and comply with it; they do not approve it.
whyNot.3: The administrator applies the measures; they do not commit the organization.

questions.prompt: A SOC analyst follows the instruction "in case of a ransomware alert, call the systems on-call, then isolate the workstation, then open an incident". Which document is the analyst applying?
questions.explanation: An ordered series of steps to carry out is a procedure.

whyNot.0: A guideline would not be a mandatory instruction.
whyNot.1: The policy does not detail steps.
whyNot.3: A baseline describes a minimum configuration, not a response to an alert.

questions.prompt: Against which standard does an organization get its information security management system certified?
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 contains the ISMS requirements: it is the certification standard.

whyNot.0: ISO/IEC 27005 guides risk management.
whyNot.2: ISO/IEC 27002 is a guide to implementing controls; you do not get certified against it.
whyNot.3: ISO/IEC 27000 gives the overview and vocabulary.

questions.prompt: How many controls does Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 contain?
questions.explanation: The 2022 version has 93 controls grouped into 4 themes.

whyNot.0: 133 was the number of controls in the 2005 version.
whyNot.1: 42 is the number of measures in ANSSI's hygiene guide.

questions.prompt: What are the four themes of Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022?
questions.explanation: The 93 controls are grouped into organizational (37), people (8), physical (14) and technological (34) controls.

whyNot.0: These are NIST CSF functions.
whyNot.2: These are security properties, not the themes of Annex A.
whyNot.3: These are control functions, not the themes of Annex A.

questions.prompt: Which ISO/IEC 27001 document lists the Annex A controls, states which are applied and justifies the exclusions?
questions.explanation: The Statement of Applicability is mandatory and justifies the inclusion or exclusion of each control.

whyNot.0: The risk register lists the risks; the SoA follows from it.
whyNot.1: The policy sets the principles, not the status of each control.
whyNot.3: The audit report records conformity; it does not decide on the controls.

questions.prompt: How long is an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate valid, and what happens in the meantime?
choices: Unlimited, as long as no incident occurs
5 years, with a single midpoint audit
questions.explanation: The certificate is valid for three years; surveillance audits take place during this period, followed by a recertification audit.

whyNot.0: The certificate is never unlimited.
whyNot.1: The standard duration is three years, not five.
whyNot.3: Validity is three years, and surveillance audits take place.

questions.prompt: In ISO/IEC 27001:2022, which clauses cover management review and corrective action? (2 answers)
questions.explanation: Management review and internal audit are in clause 9; nonconformities and corrective action in clause 10.

whyNot.0: Clause 7 covers resources, competence, communication and documented information.
whyNot.1: Clause 4 covers context, interested parties and scope.

questions.prompt: Which standard gives guidelines for identifying, collecting and preserving digital evidence?
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27037 covers the identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence.

whyNot.0: ISO/IEC 27035 covers incident management as a whole.
whyNot.2: ISO/IEC 27017 covers security controls for the cloud.
whyNot.3: ISO/IEC 27014 covers governance.

questions.prompt: Which standard in the 27000 family covers information security incident management?
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27035 describes incident management: preparation, detection, assessment, response, lessons learned.

whyNot.0: ISO/IEC 27002 describes security controls in general.
whyNot.3: ISO/IEC 27701 covers privacy protection.

questions.prompt: An organization excludes from its SoA the control on outsourced development, because it neither develops nor has any software developed. This exclusion is:
choices: Forbidden: all Annex A controls are mandatory
Possible if it is justified in the SoA
questions.explanation: Annex A controls are to be considered, not all applied: an exclusion is allowed if it is justified, for example by the absence of the risk.

whyNot.0: The standard requires considering each control and justifying the choices, not applying all of them.
whyNot.2: Every exclusion must be justified in the SoA.
whyNot.3: ISO certification does not depend on ANSSI; the certification body performs the audit.

questions.prompt: By what date did organizations certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2013 have to move to the 2022 version?
choices: No date: both versions remain valid
questions.explanation: The three-year transition period ended on October 31, 2025; 2013 certificates are no longer valid after that date.

whyNot.1: Certificates to the 2013 version expired at the end of the transition.
whyNot.2: This date does not match the end of the transition.
whyNot.3: The transition ended before this date.

questions.prompt: How many functions does the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 have?
questions.explanation: CSF 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Govern was added in 2.0.

whyNot.0: Four functions does not match any version of the CSF.
whyNot.3: Five functions was version 1.1, without Govern.

questions.prompt: In NIST CSF 2.0, which function does writing correlation rules in the SIEM belong to?
questions.explanation: Correlation rules are used to spot suspicious events: Detect function.

whyNot.0: Recover concerns returning to normal after the incident.
whyNot.2: Protect concerns the measures that prevent the incident.
whyNot.3: Identify concerns the inventory of assets, risks and context.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the NIST Cybersecurity Framework is correct?
choices: It replaces PCI DSS for card data
It is required by law for all European companies
It is a certifiable standard like ISO/IEC 27001
It is a voluntary framework for describing and improving one's cybersecurity level
questions.explanation: The CSF is a voluntary, non-certifiable framework, used to assess a current level, set a target and prioritize.

whyNot.0: PCI DSS is still required for card data.
whyNot.1: It is not a European legal obligation.
whyNot.2: There is no official CSF certification.

questions.prompt: An online store stores payment card numbers. Which framework do the card networks impose on it?
questions.explanation: PCI DSS applies to any entity that stores, processes or transmits payment card data.

whyNot.0: ITIL describes service management good practices.
whyNot.3: COBIT is an IT governance framework, not mandatory.

questions.prompt: A customer wants to know whether its cloud provider's controls actually worked over the past year. Which document is the most suitable?
questions.explanation: Type II assesses the operating effectiveness of controls over a period; Type I only describes their design at a point in time.

whyNot.0: Type I does not cover operation over a period.
whyNot.1: A sales document provides no audit assurance.
whyNot.2: A policy states intentions; it does not prove effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Which framework / use pairings are correct? (2 answers)
choices: PCI DSS: European law on personal data
NIST SP 800-53: detailed catalog of security and privacy controls
COBIT: catalog of technical controls of the US government
questions.explanation: ITIL describes IT service management; NIST SP 800-53 is a detailed catalog of controls.

whyNot.0: PCI DSS is an industry standard for payment cards; the European law on personal data is the GDPR.
whyNot.3: COBIT is an IT governance and management framework, published by ISACA.

questions.prompt: How many measures does ANSSI's IT hygiene guide contain?
questions.explanation: ANSSI's IT hygiene guide proposes 42 measures.

whyNot.0: 114 was the number of Annex A controls in 2013.
whyNot.3: 93 is the number of Annex A controls in ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

questions.prompt: Which risk analysis method is published by ANSSI?
questions.explanation: EBIOS Risk Manager is ANSSI's method for assessing and treating digital risks.

whyNot.0: OCTAVE was developed by the Software Engineering Institute (Carnegie Mellon).
whyNot.1: STRIDE is a threat modeling method from Microsoft.
whyNot.3: FAIR is a quantitative risk analysis method promoted by the FAIR Institute.

questions.prompt: A company wants a recognized certification of its management system, and a method to present its level simply to senior management. Which combination is the most consistent?
choices: ISO/IEC 27001 for certification, NIST CSF to present the level
NIST CSF for certification, ITIL to present the level
PCI DSS for certification, COBIT for the level
ISO/IEC 27002 for certification, SOC 2 for the level
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 is certifiable; the CSF, with its six functions, is handy for describing a current and target level.

whyNot.1: The NIST CSF is not certifiable.
whyNot.2: PCI DSS only concerns card data; it does not certify an ISMS.
whyNot.3: You do not get certified against ISO/IEC 27002, and SOC 2 is an audit report for customers, not an internal management tool.

questions.prompt: In the context of frameworks, what does "SOC 2" refer to?
choices: An audit report on a service provider's controls (AICPA)
The second version of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework
An ISO standard dedicated to security monitoring
questions.explanation: SOC 2 is an audit report defined by the AICPA on a service provider's controls, unrelated to a Security Operations Center.

whyNot.1: The current version of the NIST CSF is 2.0; it is not SOC 2.
whyNot.2: This is the classic trap: SOC 2 is not a SOC level.
whyNot.3: It is not an ISO standard.
